real text layer; questions and memo answers were extracted with pdftotext
(-layout) and read page by page against the official Marking Guidelines.
The memo is bilingual (English/Afrikaans); only the ENGLISH content is
transcribed here. Every question and sub-question is transcribed at full
fidelity; diagrams, graphs and experimental setups are described in
bracketed words. solution_method is the method the MEMO uses - the

questions.text: Multiple choice: The net force acting on an object on a horizontal surface is always … A in the direction of motion of the object. B in the direction of acceleration of the object. C zero when the object moves at constant acceleration. D increasing when the object moves at constant acceleration.

Multiple choice: A hot-air balloon is moving upwards at a constant velocity. A small stone is dropped from THE BALLOON. Which ONE of the following graphs represents the motions of the balloon and the stone? Ignore the effects of friction on the stone. [Four velocity (m·s⁻¹) versus time (s) graphs, each showing a line for the balloon and a line for the stone: A - balloon is a horizontal line at a positive velocity, stone starts above the balloon line at a higher positive velocity and decreases linearly; B - balloon is a horizontal line at a positive velocity, stone starts on the balloon line at the same positive velocity and decreases linearly, crossing the time axis to negative values; C - balloon is a horizontal line at a positive velocity, stone starts at zero and increases linearly above the balloon line; D - balloon is a horizontal line at a positive velocity, stone starts at zero and increases linearly, labelled above the balloon line.]

Multiple choice: A motor fixed to the ground is used to lift a box vertically upwards at a CONSTANT VELOCITY. [Diagram: motor on the ground with a cable lifting a box vertically.] Consider the statements below for the upward motion of the box. (i) The rate at which work is done by the motor on the box increases. (ii) The rate at which work is done by the motor on the box is constant. (iii) The mechanical energy of the box increases. (iv) The mechanical energy of the box is constant. Which of the statements above are CORRECT? A (i) and (iii) only B (ii) and (iv) only C (ii) and (iii) only D (i) and (iv) only

Multiple choice: Objects P and Q, with masses m and 2m respectively, have the same momentum. [Diagram: small sphere P and larger sphere Q.] The velocity of P is … A equal to the velocity of Q. B half the velocity of Q. C twice the velocity of Q. D four times the velocity of Q.

Multiple choice: A block moves along a rough horizontal surface while a horizontal force F of magnitude 18 N and a constant kinetic frictional force of magnitude 6 N act on it. [Diagram: block on a horizontal surface with F = 18 N acting to the right and fk = 6 N acting to the left.] Which ONE of the following combinations of ACCELERATION and NET WORK DONE ON THE BLOCK is CORRECT? A Acceleration: Constant, Net work done on the block: Increases B Acceleration: Increases, Net work done on the block: Constant C Acceleration: Increases, Net work done on the block: Increases D Acceleration: Constant, Net work done on the block: Constant

Multiple choice: A star's spectrum, observed from Earth, is red shifted. Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT? A The speed of light is increasing. B The star is moving towards Earth. C The frequency of each spectral line has increased. D The wavelength of each spectral line has increased.

Multiple choice: Three point charges, Q1, Q2 and Q3, are fixed in a straight line. Q1 is r metres from Q2, while Q3 is 2r metres from Q2, as shown in the diagram below. [Diagram: Q1, Q2 and Q3 on a straight line; distance Q1 to Q2 is r; distance Q2 to Q3 is 2r.] The magnitude of the charge on Q2 is q. The net electrostatic force on charge Q1 is zero. What is the magnitude of charge Q3 in terms of q? A (1/9)q B (1/3)q C 3q D 9q

Multiple choice: Three identical light bulbs, X, Y and Z, are connected in a circuit, as shown in the diagram below. Switch S is initially closed. Ignore the internal resistance of the battery. [Circuit: battery connected to bulb X in series; after X the circuit splits into two parallel branches, one containing bulb Y and the other containing switch S in series with bulb Z.] Switch S is now opened. How will the brightness of bulbs X and Y be affected? A Brightness of bulb X: Increases, Brightness of bulb Y: Decreases B Brightness of bulb X: Decreases, Brightness of bulb Y: Increases C Brightness of bulb X: Increases, Brightness of bulb Y: Increases D Brightness of bulb X: Decreases, Brightness of bulb Y: Decreases

Multiple choice: How does the commutator in a DC motor ensure that the coil rotates continuously in ONE direction? A By reducing friction B By converting AC to DC C By reversing the direction of the current in the coil D By maintaining electrical contact between the external and the internal circuits

Multiple choice: Light of different wavelengths is incident on a metal surface. Which ONE of the following graphs shows the CORRECT relationship between the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, Ek(max), and the inverse of the wavelength of the incident light, 1/λ? [Four graphs of Ek(max) (J) versus 1/λ (m⁻¹): A - straight line through the origin with positive gradient; B - curve increasing from the origin and levelling off; C - straight line with positive gradient starting on the positive 1/λ axis (positive x-intercept); D - straight line with negative gradient starting on the positive Ek(max) axis.]

questions.text: A block of mass 5 kg is at rest on a rough horizontal surface. When a constant force F of magnitude 18 N acts on the block at an angle θ to the horizontal, the block experiences maximum static friction. [Diagram: 5 kg block on a horizontal surface with force F = 18 N pulling upward at angle θ above the horizontal.] 2.1 State Newton's Second Law of Motion in words.
questions.memo_answer: When a net/resultant force acts on an object, the object will accelerate in the direction of the force and the acceleration is directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass of the object. OR: The net/resultant force acting on an object is equal to the rate of change of momentum of the object (in the direction of the net force). (2 or 0 for the second version)
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing ALL the forces acting on the block.
questions.memo_answer: Four forces on the block: w (weight, vertically down; accepted labels Fg/Fw/weight/mg/49 N/gravitational force), N (normal force, vertically up), F (applied force 18 N at angle θ above the horizontal), fs(max) (static friction, horizontal, opposite to the horizontal component of F).
questions.memo_note: Mark awarded for label and arrow. fk not accepted as label. Any additional force(s), no arrows, or forces not making contact with the dot: max 3/4.

questions.text: The horizontal component of force F is 15 N. Calculate θ.
questions.memo_working: Fx = Fcos θ; 15 = 18 cos θ; θ = 33,56°. OR 9,95 = 15 tan θ; θ = 33,56°. OR 9,95 = 18 sin θ; θ = 33,56°. NOTE: if answer only, 1/2.

questions.text: The horizontal component of force F is 15 N. Calculate the coefficient of static friction.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 2.3.1. fs(max) = µsN; the block is in equilibrium so fs(max) = Fx = 15 N and N = mg − Fsin θ = (5)(9,8) − 18sin 33,56° = 39,05 N; 15 = µs(39,05); µs = 0,38. Marking criteria: formula fs(max) = µsN; correct substitution of fs(max); correct calculation of Fy; subtraction for the calculation of N from Fg, i.e. (5)(9,8) − (18sin 33,56°); correct final answer 0,38. NOTE: if N calculation not shown, 3/5.

questions.text: Angle θ is decreased while the magnitude of force F remains constant. How will the friction acting on the block be affected? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME. Explain the answer.
questions.memo_answer: Increases. The vertical component of F decreases; the normal force increases; µs remains constant and fs(max) is directly proportional to N.
questions.memo_note: Memo also accepts: Decreases (horizontal component of F increases; the block will move, Fnet will increase; fk < fs(max)); or Remains the same if explained with a relevant calculation in which the candidate chooses µk < µs and a θ that together with the µk value gives an answer of 15 N for fk.

questions.text: A ball is projected vertically upwards from the top of a building that is 5 m high. Ignore the effects of friction. [Diagram: building of height 5 m with a ball projected vertically upwards from the top.] The table below shows the magnitude of the velocity of the ball at THREE different times during its motion: at time 0 s the magnitude of the velocity is 15 m·s⁻¹; at time p the magnitude is 0; at time 3,36 s the magnitude is q. 3.1 Define the term free fall.
questions.memo_answer: Motion under the influence of weight/gravitational force only. (2 or 0)
questions.memo_note: Memo note: if projectile is defined, 0/2.

questions.text: Using EQUATIONS OF MOTION ONLY, calculate the value of p.
questions.memo_working: Upwards as positive: vf = vi + aΔt; 0 = 15 + (−9,8)Δt; Δt = 1,53 s. (Also accepted: −15 = 0 + (−9,8)Δt over the downward leg, or 3,06 s for the full up-down flight divided by 2.) Marking criteria: formula with Δt; correct substitution; correct final answer 1,53 s. NOTE for 3.2 and 3.3: if energy principles used, 1/3 for the final answer.

questions.text: The ball strikes the ground 3,36 seconds after it was thrown upwards. Calculate q.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 3.2. Option 1 (A to ground, upwards positive): vf² = vi² + 2aΔy; vf² = (15)² + 2(−9,8)(−5); vf = 17,97 m·s⁻¹. Option 2: vf = vi + aΔt = (15) + (−9,8)(3,36) = −17,93, so 17,93 m·s⁻¹. Other accepted routes via the highest point or the top of the building give 17,94 to 18,33 m·s⁻¹. Marking criteria: formula with vf; correct substitution; correct final answer.

questions.text: The ball bounces to a maximum height of 3 m after it struck the ground. Is the collision with the ground ELASTIC or INELASTIC? Explain the answer WITHOUT the use of calculations.
questions.memo_answer: Inelastic. The height decreased/is smaller. The velocity with which the ball strikes the ground is not the same as the velocity with which it left the ground / kinetic energy is converted to heat and sound energy / kinetic energy is NOT conserved / the kinetic energy is not the same before and after the ball strikes the ground. (ACCEPT: kinetic energy is lost.)
questions.memo_note: Memo note: do not accept any calculation as an explanation.

questions.text: Sketch a velocity versus time graph for the motion of the ball from the time it was projected until it reached the maximum height after it bounced. Show the following NUMERICAL VALUES on the graph: the initial velocity, time p and velocity q.
questions.memo_answer: Taking upwards as positive: a straight line starting at v = 15 m·s⁻¹ with constant negative gradient, cutting the time axis at t = 1,53 s and reaching −17,97 m·s⁻¹ when the ball strikes the ground; then a second parallel straight line for the motion after the bounce starting at a positive velocity smaller than 17,97 m·s⁻¹ and ending at v = 0. (Mirror image accepted with downwards positive.)
questions.memo_note: Criteria: line starts at ±15 m·s⁻¹ with opposite-sign final velocity; line cuts the time axis at the time from Q3.2; correct velocity from Q3.3 when the ball is on the ground; second line has smaller magnitude than the Q3.3 value, is parallel to the first and ends at v = 0. Accept if no contact time is shown. POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 3.2 AND 3.3.

questions.text: Cricketers at an academy conduct an experiment to determine the relationship between the contact time and the final momentum of a ball for a constant average net force. A cricket ball of mass 150 g is thrown horizontally with a certain initial velocity and is struck by a bat so that the ball moves in the opposite direction, as shown in the diagram below. The average net force acting on the ball is horizontal. [Diagram: bat striking a ball; initial velocity vi towards the bat, final velocity vf away from the bat.] The experiment is repeated using the same ball. The average net force and the initial velocity of the ball are kept constant. The contact time between the bat and the ball is changed EACH time. The results obtained are shown in the sketch graph below. [Graph: final momentum pf (kg·m·s⁻¹) versus contact time Δt (s); a straight line passes through the points (0,01; 0) and (0,03; 4,5); the value 4,5 on the pf-axis is aligned with Δt = 0,03.] 4.1 Define the term impulse.
questions.memo_answer: The product of the resultant/net force acting on an object and the time the (net) force acts on the object. OR: The product of the resultant/net force and the contact time.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Calculate the average net force acting on the ball.
questions.memo_answer: Fnet = 225 N to the right / opposite to the original direction of the ball
questions.memo_working: Option 1: Gradient = Fnet = Δpf/Δ(Δt) = (4,5 − 0)/(0,03 − 0,01) = 225 N. Options 2/3: FnetΔt = Δp applied at the two graph points: Fnet(0,01) = 0 − pi and Fnet(0,03) = 4,5 − pi; solving simultaneously gives Fnet = 225 N to the right / opposite to the original direction of the ball.

questions.text: Calculate the magnitude of the initial velocity of the ball.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM 4.2.1. FnetΔt = Δp = mvf − mvi (any form); (225)(0,03) = 4,5 − (0,15)vi; vi = −15 m·s⁻¹, so magnitude 15 m·s⁻¹. (Also accepted: (225)(0,01) = 0 − (0,15)vi; or via pi = FnetΔt subtracted from pf; or via a = Fnet/m = 1500 m·s⁻² with vf = 30 m·s⁻¹.)

questions.text: Redraw the graph in the ANSWER BOOK and label it as A. On the same set of axes, draw the graph that will be obtained when a ball with a bigger mass is used, without changing the initial velocity and average net force. Label this as B.
questions.memo_answer: Graph B is a straight line parallel to graph A (same gradient = same net force) shifted to the right: it cuts the Δt-axis at a larger contact time because the initial momentum has a larger magnitude. (2 or 0)
questions.memo_note: Memo note: if labels A and B are not indicated, 0/2. Full marks for solid lines with labels.

questions.text: A crate of mass 3 kg is at rest at point A on a frictionless horizontal surface. A constant horizontal force F of 12 N acts on the crate and moves it from point A to point B. The crate then moves down a rough plane, inclined at 20° to the horizontal. The distance from point A to point B is 7 m and from point B to point C is 6,8 m, as shown in the diagram below. [Diagram: horizontal surface from A to B (7 m) with force F = 12 N pushing the 3 kg crate to the right; at B the surface becomes a plane inclined at 20° below the horizontal going down to C (B to C is 6,8 m).] 5.1 State the work-energy theorem in words.
questions.memo_answer: The net/total work done (on an object) is equal to the change in the object's kinetic energy. OR: The work done (on an object) by a resultant/net force is equal to the change in the object's kinetic energy.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Using ENERGY PRINCIPLES ONLY, calculate the kinetic energy of the crate at point B.
questions.memo_working: Wnet = ΔEk; FΔxcos θ = Ekf − Eki (any form of the theorem); (12)(7)cos 0° = Ekf − 0; Ekf = 84 J.

questions.text: Force F is removed when the crate reaches point B. The crate then experiences a constant frictional force of 21 N as it moves down the incline. Draw a free-body diagram showing ALL the forces acting on the crate as it moves down the incline.
questions.memo_answer: Three forces on the crate: w (weight, vertically down; accepted labels Fw/Fg/mg/29,4 N/gravitational force), N (normal force, perpendicular to the incline), f (kinetic friction, 21 N, up the incline opposing the motion).
questions.memo_note: Mark awarded for label and arrow. Any additional force(s), no arrows, or forces not making contact with the dot: max 2/3.

questions.text: Using ENERGY PRINCIPLES ONLY, determine whether the crate will pass point C.
questions.memo_answer: The crate will pass point C (it can travel Δx = 7,68 m > 6,8 m down the incline before stopping; equivalently Ekf at C = 9,58 J > 0 J, or vf = 2,52 m·s⁻¹ > 0).
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM 5.2. Option 1: Wnet = ΔEk; WFg + Wfk = Ekf − Eki; mg sin θ Δx cos 0° + fk Δx cos 180° = 0 − 84; (3)(9,8)sin 20°Δx − 21Δx = −84; Δx = 7,68 m; 7,68 m > 6,8 m so the crate passes C. Option 2: with Δx = 6,8 m: (3)(9,8)sin 20°(6,8)cos 0° + (21)(6,8)cos 180° = Ekf − 84; Ekf = 9,58 J > 0 so the crate passes C. Options 3/4 use Wnc = ΔEk + ΔEp with h = 6,8 sin 20° = 2,326 m, giving the same result. Criteria: substitution for WFg; substitution for Wf; substitution for ΔEk; final answer; conclusion. NOTE: cos 70° or sin 20° accepted throughout.

questions.text: An investigation is performed to determine the relationship between the velocity of a moving sound source and the frequency of the sound detected. The siren of an ambulance produces sound with a constant frequency. The ambulance, with its siren on, moves towards a stationary sound detector (Part A) and away from the stationary sound detector (Part B) at constant velocities. The experiment is repeated for different velocities of the ambulance. The detected frequency is measured for EACH velocity. The results obtained are shown in the graph below. [Diagram: Part A - ambulance moving to the right towards a stationary sound detector; Part B - ambulance moving to the right away from a stationary sound detector.] [Graph: detected frequency (Hz) versus velocity of the ambulance (m·s⁻¹, axis marked 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30). Two straight lines start from the same point on the frequency axis: the upper line rises and passes through 1 298 Hz at 25 m·s⁻¹ (dotted lines shown); the lower line falls and passes through 1 115 Hz at 25 m·s⁻¹.] 6.1 STATE the Doppler effect.
questions.memo_answer: The change in frequency (or pitch) of the sound detected by a listener, because the sound source and the listener have different velocities relative to the medium of sound propagation. OR: An (apparent) change in (observed/detected) frequency (pitch) as a result of the relative motion between a sound source and an observer.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: For this experiment, write down the independent variable.
For this experiment, write down a controlled variable.
questions.memo_answer: Frequency/wavelength of the sound produced by the ambulance siren / fs / speed of sound / density/temperature of air / detector/listener is stationary

questions.text: What conclusion can be made for Part B of this experiment?
questions.memo_answer: As the velocity of the ambulance increases, the detected frequency decreases.

questions.text: Calculate the speed of sound in air.
questions.memo_working: Ambulance approaching (at 25 m·s⁻¹, fL = 1 298 Hz): fL = v/(v − vs) × fs, so vfs = 1 298(v − 25) ... eq (1). Ambulance moving away (fL = 1 115 Hz): fL = v/(v + vs) × fs, so vfs = 1 115(v + 25) ... eq (2). Equating (1) = (2): 1 298(v − 25) = 1 115(v + 25); v = 329,64 m·s⁻¹.

questions.text: A sphere X is placed at point A on a horizontal surface. X carries a charge of +3 x 10⁻⁷ C. Point P is r metres to the left of point A. [Diagram: point P at distance r to the left of sphere X which is at point A.] The magnitude of the electric field at point P is 1,08 x 10⁶ N·C⁻¹. 7.1 Describe an electric field.
questions.memo_answer: A region of space in which an electric charge experiences a force. (2 or 0)

questions.text: Draw the electric field pattern due to the charge on sphere X.
questions.memo_answer: Field lines radially outward from the positive sphere, with arrows pointing away from the sphere.
questions.memo_note: Criteria: direction; field lines radially outward. Deduct 1 mark if two or more field lines are inside the sphere / do not touch the sphere / cross each other. If more than one charge drawn: 0/2.

questions.text: Show, by means of a calculation, that r = 0,05 m.

Sphere Y, carrying a charge of −5 x 10⁻⁷ C, is now fixed at point P and sphere Z, carrying a charge of −4 x 10⁻⁷ C, is fixed 0,04 m to the right of sphere X. [Diagram: Y (−5 x 10⁻⁷ C) at distance r to the left of X (+3 x 10⁻⁷ C, at point A); Z (−4 x 10⁻⁷ C) at 0,04 m to the right of X.] The NET FORCE acting on sphere X is 0,0427 N at point A. Is the surface frictionless? Choose from YES or NO. Explain the answer by means of a calculation.
questions.memo_answer: No. The net electrostatic force is FXZ − FXY = 0,68 − 0,54 = 0,14 N, which is greater than / not equal to the given net force of 0,0427 N (so friction of 0,0923 N acts).
questions.memo_working: FXY = kQXQY/r² = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁷)(5 x 10⁻⁷)/(0,05)² = 0,54 N. FXZ = kQXQZ/r² = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁷)(4 x 10⁻⁷)/(0,04)² = 0,68 N. Net electrostatic force = 0,68 − 0,54 = 0,14 N. Since 0,14 N ≠ 0,0427 N, the surface is not frictionless (0,0427 = 0,14 − f gives f = 0,0923 N). NOTE: ignore if negative charges are substituted.

questions.text: Sphere Y is brought into contact with sphere X, and is placed back in its original position. How will the magnitude of the force that sphere X now exerts on sphere Y be affected? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.

Two identical headlights, L1 and L2, and a starter motor, M, of a car are connected to a battery, as shown in the circuit diagram below. The resistance of each headlight is 12 Ω, while the resistance of the starter motor is 0,1 Ω. The emf (Ɛ) and internal resistance (r) of the battery are unknown. The ammeters and the connecting wires have negligible resistance, while the voltmeter has a high resistance. Switches S1 and S2 are initially open. [Circuit: battery (emf Ɛ, internal resistance r) in the central branch with ammeter A1 to its left and ammeter A2 to its right on the main top conductor; headlights L1 (12 Ω) and L2 (12 Ω) are connected in parallel with each other on the left side, in series with switch S1 and ammeter A1; a voltmeter V is connected across the battery; the starter motor M (0,1 Ω) is on the right side in series with switch S2 and ammeter A2.] 8.1 Define the term emf.
questions.memo_answer: Maximum/total energy provided / work done by a battery/cell per unit/coulomb of charge passing through it. (2 or 0)

questions.text: Switch S1 remains open while switch S2 is closed. The reading on ammeter A2 is 120 A. Calculate the reading on the voltmeter.
Switch S1 is now closed and switch S2 is opened. The power dissipated by each headlight is 15 W. Calculate the current passing through L1.
questions.memo_working: P = I²R; 15 = I²(12); I = 1,12 A. (Also accepted: P = V²/R gives V = 13,42 V, then P = VI or V = IR gives I = 1,12 A.)

questions.text: Write down the reading on ammeter A1.
Calculate the emf of the battery.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 8.2 AND 8.3.2. Rp for the headlights: 1/Rp = 1/12 + 1/12, Rp = 6 Ω. With S1 closed and S2 open: Ɛ = I(R + r) = 2,24(6 + r). With S1 open and S2 closed: Ɛ = 120(0,1 + r). Equating: 2,24(6 + r) = 120(0,1 + r); r = 0,012 Ω. Then Ɛ = 2,24(6 + 0,012) = 13,46 V (or Ɛ = 120(0,1 + 0,012) = 13,47 V). Option 2 uses Ɛ = 12 + 120r and Ɛ = 13,42 + 2,24r (from V = 13,42 V across the headlights), giving 13,45 - 13,47 V.

questions.text: Both switches are now closed. How will the reading on ammeter A1 be affected? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME. Explain the answer WITHOUT the use of a calculation.
questions.memo_answer: Decrease. Total/external resistance decreases; total current increases; V(internal) increases; voltage across the light bulbs decreases / V(external) decreases.
questions.memo_note: Memo note: calculation given as explanation 1/5. Memo also accepts (max 3/5): Increases - initial reading of A1 = 0 A when switch S1 is open; now with both switches closed current flows through the circuit (only if the explanation refers to the Q8.2 situation).

questions.text: An AC generator operates a fan. The directions of the rotation of the coil and the induced current are shown in the simplified diagram below. [Diagram: rectangular coil between two magnet poles, the right-hand pole labelled Z; the rotation direction is shown by a curved arrow at the top of the coil and the induced current direction by an arrow on the coil; the coil ends connect via two slip rings and brushes to an external circuit containing a voltmeter V and a fan.] 9.1 Define the term rms potential difference.
questions.memo_answer: The AC potential difference/voltage that produces/dissipates the same amount of energy as an equivalent DC potential difference/voltage.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark. If DC written first / energy or heating effect omitted / alternating current defined: 0/2.

questions.text: What is the polarity of the magnet at Z?

The resistance of the fan is 60 Ω and the maximum potential difference produced by the generator is 311,11 V. Calculate the cost of operating the fan for 1,5 hours if the cost of electricity is R3,33 per kWh.
questions.memo_working: Vrms = Vmax/√2 = 311,11/√2 = 219,99 V. Pave = Vrms²/R = (219,99)²/60 = 806,59 W = 0,80659 kW. Cost = PΔt x tariff = 0,80659(1,5)(3,33) = R4,03. (Equivalently E = PΔt = 1,21 kWh and cost = E x tariff = 1,21(3,33) = R4,03.)

questions.text: The voltage versus time graph for this generator is given below. [Graph: voltage (V) versus time (s); one full cosine-shaped cycle starting at a positive maximum, passing through zero, reaching a negative minimum and returning to the positive maximum at t = 4 s.] Redraw this graph in the ANSWER BOOK and label it as A. On the same set of axes, draw the graph for ONE rotation of the coil when the speed of rotation is doubled. Label this as graph B.
questions.memo_answer: Graph B: a cosine graph with amplitude bigger than that of graph A and period half of A (one full cycle in 2 s).
questions.memo_note: Criteria: amplitude of graph B bigger than that of graph A; period of B is half of A; correct shape and one cycle (cosine graph).

questions.text: State ONE way in which this generator can be changed to a DC generator.
questions.memo_answer: By replacing the slip rings with a split ring commutator / split ring / commutator.

questions.text: Learners conduct an experiment to determine whether electrons will be emitted from the surface of different metals when light with a single frequency is incident on the metal. The maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons are measured when light of frequency 1,045 x 10¹⁵ Hz is used. The results obtained are shown in the table below. [Table: Zinc - electrons emitted Yes, maximum kinetic energy 0; Sodium - Yes, 2,53 x 10⁻¹⁹ J; Caesium - Yes, 3,50 x 10⁻¹⁹ J; Metal M - No, no value.] 10.1.1 Define the term work function.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_answer: Minimum energy needed for the electrons to be emitted from the metal surface.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark. If threshold frequency defined: 0/2.

questions.text: Write down the threshold frequency of zinc.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials

questions.text: How does the work function of sodium compare to that of caesium? Choose from SMALLER THAN, GREATER THAN or EQUAL TO. Explain the answer.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_answer: Greater than. The maximum kinetic energy of electrons from sodium is smaller; E is constant / the same frequency (light) is used, so since Ek(max) is smaller, W0 is larger.

questions.text: Light of the same frequency, but with a higher intensity, is now incident on metal M. Will electrons now be ejected? Choose from YES or NO. Give a reason for the answer.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_answer: No. The intensity of light does not have any effect on the ejection of electrons for metal M OR the frequency of light has not changed / the energy of a photon has not changed.

questions.text: The energy diagram below (NOT drawn to scale) shows the electron energies in different energy levels, E1, E2 and E3, of a certain atom. [Energy level diagram with increasing energy upwards: E1 = 1,3 x 10⁻¹⁹ J; E2 = 5,1 x 10⁻¹⁹ J; E3 = 5,7 x 10⁻¹⁹ J.] An electron of this atom moves from E3 to E1. Photon X is emitted. Calculate the frequency of photon X.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_working: E = hf; 5,7 x 10⁻¹⁹ − 1,3 x 10⁻¹⁹ = (6,63 x 10⁻³⁴)f; f = 6,64 x 10¹⁴ Hz. (Accept E3 − E1 or E1 − E3; f must be positive.)

questions.text: Is it possible for a photon with an energy of 2,5 x 10⁻¹⁹ J to be emitted from this atom? Choose from YES or NO. Give a reason for the answer.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_answer: No. The energy does not correspond to any transition in this atom.
